chapter: New Orleans second line and Armstrong
title: The second line, rough New Orleans wards, and his mother's support
summary: He describes following second-line parades, dangerous wards, the Didn't He Ramble tune, whistling for Oliver, and his debt to his mother.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs

blocks.x: The first little band I played in. So I was going to ask a little bit to you about the parades and the second line.

Yeah, well the second line, the second line. I guess I just always was crazy about music. Doing that whistling and going on I did. I guess it just was destined for me to be a musician. I believe in predestination. I believe when a person is first born, that is like a big book, there's so much he's supposed to accomplish in life, you understand? And then leave this world. Now the way I used to whistle and take the sticks and pound and go on like that, and hear that music, I could follow the music for miles. It's a funny thing about music, I guess that's why they have these bands in the Army. You can march miles by music and you don't get tired. You see what I'm talking about? Now I'd march all the way down to the Seven Ward, from the 12th Ward to the Seven Ward, and the only reason I'd come back with the boys was to run me back. You had to fight when you'd go down in the Seven Ward, see? Or the Third Ward was supposed to be one of the worst in New Orleans. They called that the battlefield. See? That's where Lewis from the Third Ward was. They called that the battlefield, around Pedilla Street, Gravy Street. Well you know what went on there around Gravy and Pedilla and even Cross Canal Street, you read about it. The red light and everything, see? Well next to the, around Iberville and Vien, well we used to sneak in there and be run out, you know what they had there. Well when you come around Gravy Street, around Saratoga, Liberty and all around there, that's the parish prison there, that prison there, see it's torn down now, they don't have any more of that. So they all were. Well it was rough and tough around there. But when we hit around there, somebody would walk up and sock us and start us on the way, maybe it'd be six or seven of us, or maybe it'd be twenty of those. But them fellas would play that Diddy Ramble. Diddy Ramble.
Oh Diddy Ramble. Oh diddy Ramble. Oh diddy Ramble around the town. To the little butchie cut him down.

Oh diddy Ramble. Well you guys would be coming along, diddy Ramble, and they're wibble and they're wibble and bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo You see what I'm talking about? That's called the second line. The second line was outnumbered the procession of the other wives. See what I'm talking about? And so I started doing that and I always did, humming around, I guess my mother could see it. And so I owe a lot to my mother. I stuck with it until she died Bill. I owe a lot to my mother.

My mother started to call me playing music. I never would have got one myself, and then she had the little horn on the bed, I never would forget that. And I stuck with it until she passed. And so that's all I could do. But I guess she could see that I wanted to play music. She could see. I used to could whistle, so I'd whistle anything anybody played, and so could Snagg's Joan. And Joe Oliver used to have me to whistle to get ideas from me. Now you might not believe that. So he had me and Snagg's to whistle, and a couple of nights Joe would turn the horn to we even play it. That's what he really would do. That's how good I used to whistle. And so I started from all around, must have been eight or nine years old, I began to run behind them bands.
